---
title: Reading Input
---

Arguments are fixed before a script starts. You type them, you press Enter, and
from then on the script is on its own.

Sometimes that is not enough. A script may need to ask a question while it is
running, or work through more text than anyone would want to type on one line.
Both of those come in the same way: through **standard input**, the channel a
pipe feeds.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

* ask a question and read the answer
* feed the same script from a pipe instead
* read every line of input with a `while` loop
* write a filter of your own

And the one idea to hold on to from the start: **a script cannot tell whether
its input was typed at the keyboard or piped in.**

## Asking a question

The `read` command takes one line of input and puts it in a variable:

```{.bash filename="ask.sh"}
echo "What is your name?"
read name
echo "Hello, $name!"
```

Run it, and the script stops after the question and waits:

```session
$ bash ask.sh
What is your name?
alice
Hello, alice!
```

The middle line there is not output. It is what you typed, showing on the
screen as you typed it, and the script carried on when you pressed Enter.

Notice that `read name` has no `$` in front of the name. That is right: `$name`
would mean the value, and `read` is being told which variable to put a value
*into*. It is the same distinction as `name=alice`, which also has no `$`.

## The same script, fed by a pipe

Now try the script without typing anything at all:

```session
$ echo bob | bash ask.sh
What is your name?
Hello, bob!
```

Nobody was asked. `echo bob` produced a line, the pipe carried it to the
script, and `read` took it - just as it took the line from the keyboard a
moment ago.

`read` does not know or care where the line came from. It reads standard input,
and standard input is the keyboard only because nothing else has been put
there. Put a pipe there instead and the same script works unchanged.

The question is still printed, which looks odd but is honest: `echo` writes to
the screen and has nothing to do with standard input. Scripts meant to be used
both ways often keep the question anyway, since it costs nothing.

## Reading everything

One `read` takes one line. To handle a whole stream you need to keep reading
until there is nothing left, and for that the shell has `while`.

Here is a script that turns whatever it is given into a Markdown list, by
putting a `*` in front of every line:

```{.bash filename="make-list.sh"}
while read line
do
    echo "* $line"
done
```

```session
$ seq 3 | bash make-list.sh
* 1
* 2
* 3
```

`while` is `if`'s repeating cousin. It runs a command, and if that command
succeeded it does the lines between `do` and `done` and then tries again, over
and over, until the command fails.

The command here is `read line`. It succeeds every time it gets a line, and
fails when the input runs out - which is exactly when the loop should stop.
Three lines came in from `seq`, so the loop ran three times.

The quotes around `"* $line"` matter more than usual here. Without them the
shell would see a bare `*` and fill in the names of the files in the current
directory, and `echo` would print those instead of a bullet.

## A filter of your own

Look again at what we just built. `make-list.sh` reads lines from standard
input, writes to standard output, and does not care who is on either end of it.
That is the whole description of a filter, so it takes its place in a pipeline
like any other command - and what comes out can be sent to a file:

```session
$ seq 5 | bash make-list.sh > list.md
```

```session
$ cat list.md
* 1
* 2
* 3
* 4
* 5
```

There is nothing special about the commands that came with the machine. They
read standard input and write standard output, and now so does yours.

## Summary

| What you write | What it means |
|----------------|---------------|
| `read x` | takes one line of standard input and puts it in the variable `x` |
| `while` ... `do` ... `done` | repeat the lines as long as the command succeeds |
| `while read x` | repeat once for each line of input, stopping at the end |
| `echo hi \| bash s.sh` | the script's standard input is the pipe, not the keyboard |

And the one idea to carry forward: `read` takes a line from standard input, and
a script cannot tell whether that line was typed at the keyboard or arrived
through a pipe. That is what lets a script of your own stand in a pipeline
beside any other command.
